title: Not a breadth problem: where the damage is
body: The obvious story of the week was an AI unwind, and the index numbers support it: QQQ fell 1.2% on Friday and is down 6.6% over the past month while SPY is down 2.3%. But the model's internals say this is not broad risk aversion. Equal-weight stocks are beating the cap-weighted index, with RSP/SPY up 2.6% over three months, and that factor actually improved this week, from a contribution of +0.023 to +0.031. High-yield credit against Treasuries has barely moved, at -0.4% over three months. What has broken is narrow and specific: semiconductors against the S&P are down 16.1% over three months, and consumer discretionary against staples is down 5.7%. The damage sits in the AI complex and the consumer, not in the market's breadth and not yet in credit.

The stocks score finished at 0.055, up from 0.029 five sessions ago but down from 0.257 a month ago. Day over day only two groups moved at all: trend took 0.017 off the score as SPY slipped relative to both its 50-day and 200-day averages, and momentum added 0.006 back as the six-month return improved. Everything else was flat. The more useful number is the counterfactual. The single largest positive contributor is SPY standing 3.1% above its 200-day average, worth +0.067 on its own. Strip that one factor out and the score is roughly -0.01. The call is still comfortably above the -0.10 line that cuts exposure, but almost the entire cushion is price being above its long trend, which is the input that disappears fastest in a decline.

None of the three desks changed state this week. The stocks desk remains fully invested, 0.155 above the score that would cut it, and there is a second layer behind that: the macro group reads -0.204 against the -0.25 gate it would have to clear for a negative score to mean cash rather than half exposure. So even a break below the line would currently produce 50% invested, not zero. The Bitcoin desk remains half invested, with its score at -0.084 against a -0.15 cut, down from +0.034 five sessions ago. The move there was real: trend flipped from +0.111 to -0.138 as price lost its 20-week average, and momentum fell from -0.243 to -0.412 with the 14-day RSI at 29.8. The high-beta satellite is also half invested on its most recent report, with a relative-strength score of -0.931 and the basket down 15.9% over three months against SPY's 2.3%.

October producer prices came in at 0.3% on the month against 0.4% expected, which reads as a friendly print. The model does not read PPI. What it does read, and what the week confirmed, is less friendly. CPI is running at 3.7% year over year, still under the 4% ceiling that keeps the desk's post-selloff re-entry rule available. The three-month Treasury bill is at 4.05% and up 0.44 of a point over six months, which holds the Fed-easing factor at exactly zero. The ten-year is at 5.13% and the 10-year-minus-3-month curve is 1.08 points positive, an un-inversion that scores a full -1.00 and is the heaviest single negative in the macro group at -0.045. Stated plainly: an economy strong enough to keep the Fed tightening is a headwind for this portfolio, and this week made that marginally worse rather than better.

Here is the reading that cuts against the week's mood. University of Michigan consumer sentiment at 48.1 is the second-largest positive contributor in the whole model, at +0.025, because it enters as a contrarian input. The worse households say they feel, the more constructive this framework becomes. Anyone treating the collapse in sentiment as another bearish datapoint has the sign backwards here. The same logic runs through the volatility group, where a VIX at 19.3 scores zero rather than negative, because it is neither calm enough to signal complacency nor panicked enough to signal capitulation.

The concrete level to watch is SPY at $725.86, which is 3.8% below Friday's close. That is the price the stocks desk's own engine says would move it to half exposure if held for five sessions with every other input unchanged. In flagship weights, crossing it turns SPY 35% and QQQ 25% into 17.5% and 12.5%, leaving the portfolio 55% invested with 45% in Treasury bills. On the other side, Bitcoin would need $87,380, some 22.4% above its last close, to reach full exposure, and there is no Bitcoin downside level inside the grid the engine tested, so its zero-exposure state is not close either.

Crash watch is unchanged at 5 of 10 conditions on, status Warning. The newer confirmation set has 2 of its 3 conditions on: only 33% of nine major risk assets are above their 200-day averages, and that share has fallen 33 points in three months. The credit leg is not on. The caveat belongs in the same breath as the number: these are candidate signals on a forward test, selected from far more tests than there were events, fitted against only seven SPY declines of 10% or more since October 2006, unvalidated, and they change no exposure in any desk.

The calendar ahead is thin on model inputs and heavy on market events. Retail sales for October land on November 17, the minutes of the October 27-28 Fed meeting on November 18, and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, October PCE inflation and the Beige Book all on November 25. None of those four feed a model input directly. The two that do are further out: the November jobs report on December 4, which carries the unemployment rate, and November CPI on December 10, which carries the inflation reading that governs the re-entry rule discussed above.

The flagship's live record stands at -3.18% since inception on October 26 against the S&P 500's -0.95%, across 15 sessions, with a worst drawdown of 5.4% against the index's 5.1%. Fifteen sessions is too short to judge. Everything before October 26 on this site is a backtest, computed with hindsight from rules chosen with that history in view.
